analogy.p: Imagine particles as dancers who can only ‘react’ when two dancers bump into each other hard enough. Putting more dancers on the same floor (higher concentration or pressure) means more bumps per minute. Making the dancers move faster (higher temperature) means they bump more often and with more force, so more bumps are hard enough to count. Chopping a big block of dancers into individuals (greater surface area) means all of them can meet partners instead of only those on the edge. The analogy breaks down because real particles are not choosing partners and the collisions that count must also have the right orientation, which dancers do not need.

bullets: **Calculate the mean rate** of reaction from the quantity of reactant used or the quantity of product formed, divided by time taken.
**Units:** g/s, cm³/s and (Higher tier) mol/s; rate can also be expressed using the equations above with any unit of quantity.
**Draw and interpret graphs** of quantity of product (or reactant) against time, including using the gradient.
**Higher tier:** draw a **tangent** to a curve and use its gradient to find the rate at a specific time.
**Explain the effect** of concentration, pressure (gases), surface area (solids), and temperature on rate, using ideas about particles colliding.
**Catalysts:** know that they change the rate of reaction without being used up (the detail is a separate spec point).
**Surface area to volume ratio:** calculate and compare the ratio for different sized cubes and explain what it means for rate.
**Required practical** on rate (measuring rate by gas volume or colour/turbidity change) is its own spec point but uses all these ideas.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Chemistry topic 4.6.1 (Rate of reaction) asks you to do three connected things: **calculate** the rate of a reaction, **interpret and draw graphs** of quantity against time, and **explain how and why** changing concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature (and adding a catalyst) changes the rate. It is Paper 2 content and it is examined with calculations, graph work and extended answers, so a top-grade student must be able to do all of it fluently. At Higher tier you also use **tangents** to find the rate at a point on a curve, and work in **mol/s**.

bullets: **Rate of reaction = the amount of reactant used or product formed per unit time.**
The quantity can be a **mass (g)**, a **volume of gas (cm³)** or, at Higher tier, a **number of moles (mol)**.
A **faster** reaction takes a **shorter time** to reach the same amount of product; rate is roughly **proportional to 1 ÷ time**.
Rate is highest at the **start** (reactant concentration is highest) and falls as reactants are used up; it becomes **zero** when a reactant has run out.
The **limiting reactant** is the reactant that runs out first and decides the final amount of product.
Rate is about **how fast**, not **how much**: the total amount of product depends on the amount of limiting reactant, not on the rate.
Industry wants a **fast enough** rate to be economical, but not so fast that the reaction is unsafe or hard to control.
core.h: What ‘rate of reaction’ means and why we measure it
core.p: The **rate of a reaction** tells you how fast reactants are turned into products. Some reactions are very slow (rusting, weathering of rocks), some are moderate (magnesium dissolving in acid) and some are very fast (explosions). Chemists and industry care about rate because it controls how much product can be made per hour and how safe a process is. Rate is measured as a **change in quantity per unit time**: either how much reactant disappears or how much product appears in a certain time.

bullets: **Mean rate = quantity of reactant used ÷ time taken.**
**Mean rate = quantity of product formed ÷ time taken.**
**Rearrangements:** quantity = rate × time and time = quantity ÷ rate.
**Units:** g/s if the quantity is in grams; cm³/s if it is a gas volume in cm³; mol/s if it is in moles. If time is in minutes the unit is per minute (e.g. g/min).
**Part of a reaction:** between 20 s and 40 s, rate = (V at 40 s − V at 20 s) ÷ (40 − 20). Example: (34 − 22) ÷ 20 = 0.6 cm³/s.
**Check significant figures:** give the answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data, or follow the question.
If a question gives two rates, **compare** them by dividing or subtracting, and say which is faster.
core.p: The **mean (average) rate** is found by dividing the change in quantity by the time over which the change happened. It tells you the average speed over a period but hides the fact that the rate changes during the reaction. To find the rate over only part of the reaction, use the **change** in quantity between two times, not the total. Always include the correct **unit**, which is the unit of quantity divided by the unit of time. These equations are **not** given on the AQA equation sheet, so you must learn them.

bullets: **Steepest part** = fastest rate (usually at the start, at time 0).
**Curve flattens** = rate falls because reactants are being used up; the **horizontal line** = reaction finished (at least one reactant has all reacted).
**Same final height, steeper curve** = faster reaction but the same amount of limiting reactant (e.g. higher temperature, higher concentration, powder, catalyst).
**Lower final height** = less limiting reactant (e.g. less acid, or less magnesium) was used, not just a change in rate.
**Time to finish** = the time at which the line first becomes horizontal; compare two experiments by reading the time to reach the same volume.
**Reactant against time:** starts high, falls steeply, then flattens at zero (if all reacts) or at a non-zero value (if the reaction does not go to completion).
**Drawing graphs:** label axes with quantity and unit, choose a scale that uses over half the grid, plot points exactly, and draw a smooth best-fit curve (not dot-to-dot).
core.p: A graph of **quantity of product against time** is the standard way of showing how a reaction progresses. The **gradient** (steepness) at any point is the **rate** at that moment. The line starts steep because the concentration of reactants is highest, then becomes less steep as reactants are used up, and finally becomes **horizontal** when the reaction has stopped. A graph of **reactant against time** falls instead of rises but follows the same logic. You should be able to **sketch** these graphs and to read information from them.

bullets: **Step 1:** mark the time you are asked about on the x-axis and go up to the curve.
**Step 2:** place a ruler so that it touches the curve **only at that point** and the gap between the ruler and the curve is the same on both sides.
**Step 3:** draw the straight line, long enough to cross over half the graph (a bigger line gives a smaller percentage error).
**Step 4:** pick two points **on the tangent** (not on the curve) far apart; draw a right-angled triangle.
**Step 5:** gradient = **rise ÷ run** = change in y ÷ change in x, with units y-unit/x-unit (e.g. cm³/s).
A tangent at **time 0** gives the **initial rate**; tangents later on are shallower because the reaction slows.
Mark schemes usually allow a **tolerance**, so a neat tangent with correct working will earn the mark even if the answer differs slightly.
If asked to **compare** the rate at two times, draw two tangents and compare the gradients.
core.h: Higher tier: finding the rate at a point using a tangent
core.p: On a curved graph the rate is changing all the time, so the mean rate does not tell you the speed at one particular moment. The **gradient of the curve at that point** gives the rate at that instant. Because the curve is not a straight line, you find this gradient by drawing a **tangent**: a straight line that just touches the curve at the chosen point and has the same steepness as the curve there. You then find the gradient of the tangent by drawing a large right-angled triangle. Examiners give marks for the tangent, for a large triangle and for correct reading of rise and run.

bullets: **Mass to moles:** n = mass (g) ÷ Mr.
**Gas volume to moles (RTP):** n = V (dm³) ÷ 24, or n = V (cm³) ÷ 24 000.
**Mean rate (mol/s)** = moles of product formed (or reactant used) ÷ time (s).
**Convert from g/s** by dividing the rate by Mr; **convert from cm³/s** by dividing by 24 000.
**Standard form:** answers are often very small, e.g. 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol/s; use your calculator’s EXP button.
**Using the equation:** the mole ratio in the balanced equation tells you how the rate of formation of one product compares with the rate of use of a reactant.
Always show the **conversion step**; it often earns a mark on its own.
core.p: Higher tier students may need to give a rate in **moles per second**. This links rate to **quantitative chemistry**: you convert the mass or gas volume to moles first, then divide by time. If the quantity is a mass, use **n = m ÷ Mr**. If it is a volume of gas at room temperature and pressure, use **n = V ÷ 24** with V in dm³ (or V ÷ 24 000 with V in cm³), because one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP. Then rate = moles ÷ time. Check the unit each time.

bullets: **Gas collected:** measure the **volume of gas** produced every 10 s using a **gas syringe** or an upturned measuring cylinder over water; plot volume against time.
**Mass lost:** if a gas escapes, a reaction flask on a **balance** loses mass; record mass every 10 s (use a cotton wool plug to stop spray).
**Colour change/turbidity:** for sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, measure the **time for a cross under the flask to disappear** as sulfur precipitates; rate ∝ 1 ÷ time.

**Variables:** change one **independent variable** (e.g. concentration), measure the **dependent variable** (time or volume) and keep the others (temperature, volume, mass, surface area) constant as **control variables**.
**Repeat** the experiment to spot anomalies and calculate a mean, which improves reliability.
**Safety:** wear eye protection; HCl is an irritant; do not stopper a flask that releases gas without a vent.
**Limitations:** the cross method relies on a person’s judgement of when the cross vanishes; gas syringes can stick.
core.h: How rate is measured in practice (link to the required practical)
core.p: The measurement chosen depends on what the reaction does. You need a quantity that **changes measurably with time**, a way to measure the **time**, and a fair test with only one variable changed. These methods and the required practical on rate are a separate spec point, but you must understand the principle in order to interpret questions on data and graphs.

bullets: **Increasing concentration** → more particles per unit volume → **more frequent collisions** → **faster rate**.
**Concentration units:** mol/dm³ or g/dm³; 2 mol/dm³ has twice as many particles per dm³ as 1 mol/dm³.
The **proportion** of collisions that are successful does not change; the **number of collisions per second** does.
As the reaction proceeds, concentration of reactants **falls**, so the rate **slows down**; this is why curves flatten.
For a reaction where **concentration is doubled**, the rate is often (but not always) roughly doubled; this is not an exam requirement.
**Dilution** has the opposite effect: fewer particles per unit volume, fewer collisions, slower reaction.
**Common test:** magnesium and hydrochloric acid of different concentrations: higher acid concentration gives faster gas production and a steeper graph.
**Do not** write that particles ‘have more energy’ for a concentration change.
core.p: If you increase the **concentration** of a reactant in solution, there are **more particles in the same volume**, so the particles are closer together. They collide **more often**, which means more **successful collisions per second** and a **higher rate**. The particles do not move any faster; there are just more of them in the same space. On a graph, a higher concentration gives a **steeper curve**; if the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged the final volume is the same, but if the concentration of the limiting reactant is higher (with the same volume of solution) there is more reactant, so more product.

bullets: **Increase in pressure** (gases) → particles squashed closer → **more collisions per second** → **higher rate**.
**Higher pressure** is equivalent to **higher concentration** for a gas.
**No effect** on the **energy** of particles; only the frequency of collisions.
**Industrial relevance:** gas-phase reactions (such as the Haber process) are run at high pressure to speed up the reaction and (as you learn later) to affect the yield.
**Decrease in pressure** → fewer collisions → slower reaction.
**Solid or liquid reactants** are not noticeably affected by pressure.
Exam link: if a question mentions a **gas** and asks about pressure, explain with ‘particles closer together’ and ‘more frequent collisions’.
core.p: For reactions involving **gases**, increasing the **pressure** pushes the gas particles into a **smaller volume**, so there are more particles per unit volume. This is exactly like increasing concentration: the particles are **closer together**, collide **more frequently**, and the rate **increases**. Pressure has **no effect** on reactions of solids or liquids because these are not compressible in the same way. A pressure change only matters if at least one of the reactants is a gas.

bullets: **Increasing surface area** (smaller pieces) → more particles exposed → **more collisions per second** → **faster rate**.
**Example:** marble chips (calcium carbonate) react slowly with acid, but powdered marble reacts rapidly; the **same total volume of gas** is produced eventually if the mass is the same.
**Surface area to volume ratio (SA:V):** for a cube of side L, SA = 6L², V = L³, so SA:V = 6 ÷ L; smaller L gives a bigger ratio.
**Worked comparison:** side 1 cm → SA 6 cm², V 1 cm³ → 6:1; side 2 cm → SA 24, V 8 → 3:1; side 3 cm → SA 54, V 27 → 2:1.
**Cutting a cube** into smaller cubes increases the **total** surface area for the same total volume.
**Dust explosions:** fine powders (flour, coal dust, custard powder, sawdust) have a huge surface area and can burn explosively in air; factories reduce risk by removing dust and avoiding sparks.
**Link to biology:** organisms with a large SA:V exchange substances faster, which is the same mathematical idea.
**Graph effect:** powder gives a steeper curve with the same final volume as chips of equal mass.
core.h: Factor 3: surface area of a solid
core.p: Reactions with a **solid** can only take place at the **surface**, because particles inside a lump cannot meet the other reactant. If you break the solid into smaller pieces, the **total surface area** increases while the **volume stays the same**, so more particles are exposed to the other reactant. This increases the **frequency of collisions** and so the **rate**. A powder therefore reacts much faster than the same mass of lumps. At Higher tier you can describe this using the **surface area to volume ratio**.

bullets: **Higher temperature** → particles have **more energy** and move **faster** → **more frequent collisions** and **more energetic collisions**.
**Activation energy** = the minimum energy particles must have when they collide for the reaction to happen.
A bigger **proportion of the particles** exceeds the activation energy at higher temperature; this is why the rate increases so much.
As a rough guide, many reactions double in rate for a **10 °C rise**; this is not an exam requirement.
**Lowering the temperature** slows reactions: refrigerators and freezers slow the reactions that make food go off.
**Safety:** very high temperatures can make reactions go out of control; industrial processes choose a **compromise** temperature.
**Graph:** higher temperature gives a **steeper** curve that reaches the **same final volume** sooner.
**Do not** say that particles ‘expand’ or ‘get bigger’ when heated; they move faster.
core.p: Increasing the **temperature** gives particles more **kinetic energy**, so they **move faster**. This has two effects. First they collide **more often**. Second, and more importantly, a larger **proportion** of collisions have energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy**, so more collisions are **successful** (lead to reaction). Both effects increase the rate, and the second effect is the bigger one. This is why a small increase in temperature can cause a big increase in rate. The final amount of product (with the same amount of limiting reactant) is unchanged.

bullets: **Catalyst** = increases rate, **not used up**, not in the overall equation, **lower activation energy**.
**Enzymes** are biological catalysts, e.g. in fermentation to make ethanol.
**Examples:** iron in the Haber process; platinum in catalytic converters; manganese(IV) oxide (MnO₂) for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
Different reactions need **different catalysts**; they are specific.
**Cost:** catalysts reduce the energy needed (cheaper) but may be expensive metals; they can become poisoned by impurities.
**On a graph:** a catalysed reaction is steeper and reaches the same final volume.
**Other ways of increasing rate** that you may meet: using a **stirrer** to mix reactants, or exposing to **light** for some reactions (not an exam requirement).
core.h: Catalysts and the other ways of changing rate
core.p: A **catalyst** is a substance that **increases the rate** of a chemical reaction **without being used up** in the reaction. It provides an **alternative reaction pathway** with a **lower activation energy**, so a larger proportion of collisions are successful. Catalysts do not change the amount of product, they are not shown in the overall equation and they can often be used again. They are covered in detail in their own spec point, but you must be able to include them in lists of factors affecting rate.

bullets: **Chain of reasoning:** change in condition → change in particle behaviour → change in number of successful collisions per second → change in rate.
**Concentration/pressure/surface area:** only change **frequency** of collisions.
**Temperature:** changes **frequency** and **energy** (more particles above the activation energy).
**Catalyst:** changes **activation energy** only (alternative pathway).
**Use the words:** ‘more **frequent** collisions’, ‘more **successful** collisions per second’, ‘**activation energy**’.
**Do not** write ‘more collisions’ alone; say ‘more collisions **per second**’.
**Do not** say reactions ‘want’ to happen or that particles ‘try’ to collide.
core.p: All of the factors above are explained using the **collision theory** idea: for a reaction to happen, particles must **collide** with **enough energy** (at least the activation energy). The **rate** depends on the **number of successful collisions per second**. A condition can increase the rate in two ways: it can make particles collide **more often** (concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature) or it can make a **greater proportion of collisions successful** (temperature, catalyst). The exam skill is to link the condition to what the particles do and then to the rate. The full treatment of collision theory is a separate spec point.

bullets: **Food in a fridge or freezer:** lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food.
**Pressure cookers:** higher pressure raises the boiling point of water so food cooks at a higher temperature (faster).
**Powdered ingredients** (such as cocoa) dissolve and react faster than lumps.
**Flour mills and coal mines:** fine dust has a huge surface area; strict controls prevent dust explosions.
**Catalytic converters:** a platinum/rhodium catalyst speeds up the removal of toxic gases from exhaust fumes.
**Industrial processes** use a compromise of temperature, pressure and catalyst to make products at a good rate and low cost.
**Fireworks:** finely ground metals burn faster and brighter than large pieces.
**Antacid tablets:** crushing the tablet increases surface area, so it neutralises stomach acid faster.
core.p: The factors that change rate are used constantly in industry, kitchens and safety design. Knowing real examples gives you something concrete to refer to in an extended answer and helps you remember each factor. They also show why rate matters: speeding up a useful reaction saves money, slowing down an unwanted one saves food or prevents explosions.

bullets: **For ‘explain why’ questions:** condition → particles → collisions per second → rate (4 linked ideas earns most marks).
**For graph comparisons:** quote numbers, e.g. ‘reaches 40 cm³ after 30 s instead of 60 s’.
**Different final heights** mean different amounts of limiting reactant; **same final height** means same amount.
**Tangent working:** show the triangle; quote rise and run; give units.
**Mean rate vs rate at a point:** mean rate uses a straight-line change between two points; tangent gives the rate at a single instant.
**Say ‘rate’** not ‘it goes quicker’; use the correct variable names.
**Check units:** g/s, cm³/s, mol/s; do not mix cm³ with dm³.
**Surface area:** ‘larger surface area’ not ‘more area’; for powders ‘more particles exposed’.
**Maths skill:** recalculate with a different method (e.g. use a second pair of points) to check a tangent gradient.
core.h: Exam technique and common graph traps
core.p: Rate questions come in three types: **calculation**, **graph interpretation** and **explanation**. A top answer shows each calculation step with units, uses specific numbers from the graph, and links every explanation to **collisions per second**. Practise setting out working neatly, and always state whether you are finding a **mean** rate or a rate at a **point**.

exam: **Define rate (1 mark):** ‘the amount of reactant used or product formed per unit time’; give units.
**Mean rate calculation (2 marks):** write quantity ÷ time, substitute, give answer with unit (1 mark method, 1 mark answer).
**Rate between two times (2–3 marks):** subtract the two readings first, then divide by the time difference.
**Higher tier tangent (3–4 marks):** tangent drawn at the right point (1), triangle with large rise and run (1), gradient calculated (1), correct unit (1).
**mol/s (2–3 marks):** convert to moles first (n = m ÷ Mr or V ÷ 24 000), then ÷ time.
**Graph sketch (2 marks):** correct curve shape that starts steeper and finishes at the same height for same amount of limiting reactant; label axes.
**Explain the effect of a factor (3–4 marks):** state the change, link to particles, link to collisions per second, state the rate result.
**Surface area (2–3 marks):** ‘powder has a larger surface area; more particles exposed; more frequent collisions’.
**Temperature (3 marks):** ‘particles move faster, collide more often, more collisions have at least the activation energy’.
**6-mark plan:** choose a method, state variable changed and controlled, say what you measure, give a result pattern, explain using collision theory.
**Always** quote units and use data from the question where it is given.

mistakes.r: Also say that more particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so a larger proportion of collisions are successful.
mistakes.w: Higher temperature means particles collide more often, so the rate is higher (nothing more).

mistakes.r: A steeper graph means a faster rate; the amount of product depends on the amount of limiting reactant (final height).
mistakes.w: A steeper graph means more product is made.

mistakes.r: A tangent touches the curve at one point; the rise and run are read from points on the tangent line.
mistakes.w: Drawing a tangent that crosses the curve, or using points on the curve for the gradient.

mistakes.r: Rate = quantity (volume, mass or moles) ÷ time; units are cm³/s, g/s or mol/s.
Increasing pressure of a gas puts the particles closer together, so there are more frequent collisions; the energy of the particles is unchanged.
mistakes.w: Increasing pressure makes particles move faster.

mistakes.r: A catalyst is not used up, does not appear in the overall equation and provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
mistakes.w: A catalyst is used up and appears in the equation.

mistakes.r: Powder has a larger surface area (more particles exposed), so there are more frequent collisions.
mistakes.w: Powder reacts faster because the particles are smaller.

mistakes.r: The curve flattens because one reactant (the limiting reactant) has been used up, so no more product can form.
mistakes.w: The curve levels off because the reaction slows down and then stops by itself.

mistakes.r: Convert mass to moles with n = m ÷ Mr, or gas volume with n = V ÷ 24 000 (cm³), then divide by time.
mistakes.w: Answers to mol/s calculations left in g/s or cm³/s.

summary: The rate of reaction is the quantity of reactant used or product formed per unit time. You must be able to calculate mean rates (g/s, cm³/s and, at Higher tier, mol/s), read and draw rate graphs (using tangents at Higher tier), and explain how concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature, plus catalysts, change the rate by changing the number of successful collisions per second.

Effect of conditions on a volume–time graph: B has the same total as A but is faster (higher concentration, temperature, surface area or catalyst); C is faster but made less product because there was less limiting reactant.
Surface area to volume ratio of cubes: smaller pieces have a larger ratio, so react faster.

terms.d: The change in quantity of a reactant used or a product formed per unit time.
The total change in quantity divided by the total time taken, giving an average over the period.
The amount of a substance in a given volume of solution, e.g. mol/dm³ or g/dm³.
The total area of the outside of a solid that is exposed and can react with another substance.
Surface area divided by volume; it increases as the pieces get smaller.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
The steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x (rise ÷ run).
The reactant that is completely used up first, so it limits the amount of product that can form.
The number of collisions between reacting particles per second.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur.
A collision between particles with at least the activation energy (and the right orientation) that results in a reaction.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
The energy a particle has because it is moving; it increases as the temperature rises.
Very rapid burning of a fine powder suspended in air, caused by the very large surface area.
Apparatus used to measure the volume of gas produced in a reaction over time.
A variable that is kept the same in an experiment so that it is a fair test.

worked.q: Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid in an open flask on a balance. The flask loses 0.44 g in 55 s as carbon dioxide escapes. (a) Calculate the mean rate in g/s. (b) Higher tier: calculate the mean rate in mol/s. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16) (4 marks)
steps: (a) Mean rate = mass lost ÷ time = 0.44 ÷ 55 = 0.0080 g/s.

worked.q: Higher tier. A tangent to a volume–time graph at 20 s passes through (5 s, 20 cm³) and (35 s, 56 cm³). Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 s in cm³/s and in mol/s (1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³). (4 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: Powdered marble has a larger surface area than the chips, so more calcium carbonate particles are exposed to the acid. This increases the frequency of collisions between reacting particles, so there are more successful collisions per second and the rate of reaction increases. The final volume of gas is the same because the same mass of marble (the amount of limiting reactant) was used.
worked.q: Equal masses of marble chips and powdered marble are added to the same volume of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration at the same temperature. The powder reacts faster. Explain why. (4 marks)
steps: The powder has a larger surface area (and larger surface area to volume ratio) than the chips.
More particles of calcium carbonate are exposed to the acid.
So there are more frequent collisions between acid particles and calcium carbonate particles.
So more successful collisions per second, so a higher rate. The total volume of gas is the same as the mass of marble is the same.
